first_impression.reaction: My daughter sent it, so I read it properly on the iPad. The opening is calm and grown-up, no silly slang. The line 'it also covers the two real choices: marrying in Serbia, or carrying the customs home' told me there would be a practical part, so I kept going, top to bottom, as I always do.

journey.quote: Serbian wedding traditions are often reduced to a list of quirks. Seen in order, they make far more sense.
journey.reaction: Sensible. Laying it out in order helps me follow what the family will expect on the day.

journey.section: Serbian wedding traditions: what the day looks like, in order
journey.quote: The church rite is set by the Serbian Orthodox Church. The folk customs around it belong to families, and no two families keep them in quite the same way.
journey.reaction: I like that it doesn't pretend to know our family better than we do. Being honest about what is fixed and what isn't makes me trust the rest more.

journey.quote: Choose your kum early. The church needs his baptism certificate as well as yours, so this is not a decision to leave until the invitations go out.
journey.reaction: Exactly the kind of practical deadline I want written down. I'll forward this bit to my husband.

journey.quote: If your family wants to include the apple, talk it through with them and with your venue well ahead, since what suits a village courtyard will not suit a city hotel.
journey.reaction: Good, a nudge to check with the venue. Saves an awkward conversation on the day.

journey.quote: You must register with local police within 24 hours of arrival, and your hotel or host normally arranges it.
journey.reaction: I didn't know that. Useful for the older relatives, and it's dated and sourced to Smartraveller, which I trust.

journey.quote: It notes unexploded landmines in the southern area bordering Kosovo and advises using well-known roads and paths there.
journey.reaction: That gave me a jolt. I appreciate the honesty, but I'd like to know whether that is anywhere near where weddings actually happen, or whether Belgrade is a world away from it.

journey.quote: Australians do not need a visa for tourist visits of up to 90 days in a 6-month period, though entry conditions can change at short notice.
journey.reaction: Fine for the visa, but nothing at all on getting elderly guests there comfortably. Flights, transfers, a church with steps, travel insurance for someone in their eighties. That's what I'd be worrying about.

journey.quote: So build the paperwork backwards. Ask the Serbian authorities whether they accept a CNI issued in Australia, and whether it needs an apostille, before you book anything.
journey.reaction: Clear and responsible. 'Before you book anything' is what I'd say to my daughter myself.

journey.quote: Smartraveller's page on getting married overseas suggests talking to a lawyer to confirm validity.
journey.reaction: Good that they don't pretend to be lawyers. I want the marriage to be legal back home without any fuss.

journey.section: Bringing Serbian customs to a wedding in Australia or overseas
journey.quote: A Saturday you love may simply not be available.
journey.reaction: Very helpful. Better to know that before anyone pays a reception deposit.

journey.section: Bringing Serbian customs to a wedding in Australia or overseas
journey.quote: One person is your single point of contact for venue, travel, vendors and payments, and the fee is agreed in writing before any work begins.
journey.reaction: This is the sentence I was looking for. One person, the fee in writing. It doesn't tell me who that person is or whether deposits to Serbian suppliers are protected, but it's the right start.

unanswered_questions: If we pay deposits to a venue or suppliers in Serbia, is that money protected, and who is responsible if a supplier lets us down?
Are contracts with Serbian suppliers in English, and are quotes given in Australian dollars?
Who do I ring if something goes wrong on the day, at 2am Belgrade time? Is there someone on the ground?
Can elderly guests with limited mobility get into the churches and venues, and who arranges airport transfers for them?
What travel insurance should older guests have for a trip to Serbia?
Who is the Wedded Advisor? Can I speak to them on the phone before anything is booked?
would_share_with: My husband, with the paperwork and kum sections highlighted
My daughter, to say yes, this is useful, let's ring them

cta_reaction.quote: If you are planning a Serbian wedding abroad, or a blended celebration in Australia, you can speak with a Wedded Advisor.
cta_reaction.why: 'Speak with' is what I want, and the fee in writing reassures me. I'd click if I knew it led to a phone call with a real person rather than a long form, and if I had some sense of how deposits and overseas suppliers are handled.

top_3_changes: Add a short, practical paragraph for older or less mobile guests travelling to Serbia: transfers, church steps, travel insurance, pointing to what to ask rather than inventing details.
Next to the Wedded Advisor sentence, say plainly what happens after you click (a phone call with a named person) and who is on hand if something goes wrong on the day.
Give the landmine note a sentence of context, for example that the advice applies to the southern border area, so a nervous parent doesn't read it as a warning about the whole trip.
